content: Human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) is a virus that targets and destroys CD4 cells, which are critical components of the immune system. Over time, if left untreated, HIV can severely weaken the immune system, leading to acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS). This condition leaves the body vulnerable to infections and certain cancers. According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), approximately 1.2 million people aged 13 years and older in the United States were living with HIV as of the end of 2019. Individuals living with HIV (PWH) are at an increased risk of developing severe complications from influenza, particularly those with very low CD4 cell counts or those not receiving antiretroviral therapy (ART). ART is the standard treatment for HIV, and while 81% of PWH in the United States were prescribed ART during 2018-2019, nearly 20% of this population remains especially vulnerable to flu-related complications. Research has shown that PWH may experience prolonged flu symptoms, an increased risk of complications, and extended viral shedding compared to individuals without HIV. Therefore, it is crucial for PWH to receive an annual flu vaccination. The flu vaccine is the most effective method of preventing influenza in PWH. Studies have demonstrated that flu vaccination reduces the risk of illness and the need for medical visits among PWH and others with compromised immune systems. Injectable flu vaccines are safe and recommended for PWH, while the live attenuated influenza vaccine (LAIV), administered as a nasal spray, is not recommended due to its use of a weakened live virus, which may pose risks to immunocompromised individuals. It is important to note that PWH with advanced HIV disease may have a reduced immune response to the flu vaccine. In some cases, healthcare providers may consider prescribing antiviral medications for flu prevention. Pneumococcal pneumonia is a serious complication of influenza that can be life-threatening. PWH should ensure they are up to date with pneumococcal vaccinations to protect against diseases such as pneumonia, meningitis, and bloodstream infections. There are two types of pneumococcal vaccines available: the pneumococcal conjugate vaccine and the pneumococcal polysaccharide vaccine. However, these vaccines should not be administered simultaneously. A healthcare provider can recommend the appropriate pneumococcal vaccine based on individual health needs. In addition to vaccination, PWH should adopt everyday preventive measures to reduce the risk of flu infection. These include avoiding contact with sick individuals, covering coughs, washing hands frequently, improving indoor air quality, and disinfecting surfaces that may harbor viruses. If a person with HIV develops flu symptoms, they should contact their healthcare provider immediately. Antiviral medications are available to treat influenza and can reduce the severity and duration of illness, as well as prevent serious complications. These medications are most effective when started within 48 hours of symptom onset. There are four FDA-approved antiviral drugs recommended by the CDC for the 2023-2024 flu season, and a prescription is required to obtain them. Flu symptoms can include fever, cough, sore throat, runny or stuffy nose, body aches, headache, chills, and fatigue. Some individuals may also experience vomiting and diarrhea, though these symptoms are more common in children. It is possible to have respiratory symptoms without a fever. Prompt treatment with antiviral drugs is especially important for PWH, as they are at higher risk of severe complications. Emergency warning signs of flu complications vary by age group. In children, these signs include difficulty breathing, bluish lips or face, chest pain, severe muscle pain, dehydration, seizures, and high fever that does not respond to medication. In adults, warning signs include shortness of breath, persistent chest pain, confusion, seizures, severe muscle pain, and worsening of chronic medical conditions. Anyone experiencing these symptoms should seek medical attention immediately. For individuals with egg allergies, flu vaccines are now considered safe regardless of the severity of the allergy. Beginning with the 2023-2024 flu season, additional precautions for those with severe egg allergies are no longer required. However, all vaccines should be administered in settings equipped to manage allergic reactions. In summary, PWH should prioritize annual flu vaccination, pneumococcal vaccination, and everyday preventive measures to reduce their risk of influenza and its complications. Prompt medical attention and antiviral treatment are essential if flu symptoms develop.
